title: Who Really Built the Pyramids?
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · Testing a belief against the evidence

hero.credit: Facsimile by Charles K. Wilkinson · The Met

objective: Students will test a common belief, that slaves built the pyramids, against the evidence in the exhibition’s first poster: the builders’ town and tombs, the diary of an inspector named Merer, and what is known of the architect Hemiunu and his crews. Setting it in the Nile’s year, they will sort sources by kind, say what each can and cannot show, and weigh a tomb painting from a later age.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Many people still repeat that slaves built the pyramids. Historians do not settle a question by repeating it: they look for evidence, ask what kind it is, and say how far it reaches. That habit protects us from easy answers about any past.

items.text: describe how the Nile shaped Egypt: the black land and the red land, and a year of three seasons
items.question: describe how the Nile shaped Egypt’s land and year?

items.text: use evidence from archaeology and written records to explain who built the pyramids
items.question: explain who built the pyramids, with evidence?

items.text: tell apart kinds of sources, and say what each can and cannot show
items.question: say what each kind of source can and cannot show?

items.text: judge how far a source from a later time can support a claim about an earlier one
items.question: judge how far a later source can support a claim?

materials: Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed: the four sources and the harvest wall
Sticky notes or scrap paper for the hook; differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **Poster 1**, *The Mysteries of Ancient Egypt*: read the chapter *Who really built the pyramids?* and its fun tidbits, from Merer’s diary to the tiny ivory statue of Khufu, just 7.5 centimetres (3 inches) tall.
**Virtual visit:** in *Tomb Explorer*, choose *The harvest* and find the chariot, the measuring rope and the scribes with the torch.

steps.title: What have you heard?
script: Before showing anything, ask students to write on a note who built the pyramids, and **where they heard it**. Collect a few answers aloud. Many will say slaves. Do not correct anyone yet: *“Today we test that answer the way a historian would: what is the evidence, and what kind of evidence is it?”*

screen.question: Who built the pyramids? Write what you have heard, and where you heard it.

steps.purpose: Surface what students already believe, and where the belief came from.
students: Write your answer on a note.
Then write where you heard it: a film, a book, a person?

steps.title: The black land and the red land
script: The civilization of ancient Egypt lasted for over three thousand years, in northeastern Africa along the Nile. Egyptians called their country **Kemet**, “the black land”, after the dark, fertile soil left by the floods; the desert beyond was **Deshret**, “the red land”. Their year had three seasons: **Akhet**, when the Nile flooded; **Peret**, the growing season; and **Shemu**, the harvest. Nilometers measured how high the river rose each year.

screen.caption: Kemet, the black land: a year of three seasons

steps.purpose: Set the scene: a land made by the Nile, and a year made by its flood.
students: Why call your own country “the black land”?
What would a farmer do in each season?

steps.title: The builders
script: Now the evidence (page 3). Contrary to popular belief, the pyramids were not built by slaves. Archaeologists have uncovered the **town and tombs** of the builders and estimate a workforce of 20,000 to 30,000 Egyptians. Khufu’s architect, **Hemiunu**, led artisans, sculptors, masons and metalworkers, many living in a settlement built for them. Inspectors like **Merer** supplied rations, tools, clothes, medical treatments and materials, and Merer’s **diary** on papyrus, found at Wadi el-Jarf in 2013, tells how the pyramids of Giza were supplied.

cells: Where the builders lived and were buried
A written record of the time
How the pyramids of Giza were supplied
Who led the work, and how it was supplied
How officials measured and recorded work

steps.purpose: Meet the evidence, and name what kind of source each one is.
students: Which of these was written at the time?
Which was dug out of the ground?

steps.title: A wall that keeps records
script: Show the harvest wall from Menna’s tomb, painted about 1396–1347 BCE. Menna was in charge of the government’s lands: surveyors measure the grain with a knotted rope, and scribes write down the harvest. Ask: *“This shows officials organizing and recording work. Can it tell us who built the pyramids?”* Leave the question open for the activity.

screen.artist: Charles K. Wilkinson, a copy of a painting in the tomb of Menna, Thebes

img.credit: Facsimile by Charles K. Wilkinson · The Met

screen.alt: A tomb painting in two rows: above, men walk through a field of ripe grain holding a long rope; below, a horse and chariot wait while workers heap grain and scribes sit writing

steps.purpose: See Egyptian officials at work, and ask what a later painting can prove.
students: Find the knotted rope. Find the scribe counting on his fingers.
Can this wall tell us who built the pyramids?

steps.title: Weigh the evidence
script: Students choose a handout. All three work from the same four sources and end with a claim backed by evidence.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Match each source to its kind, sort the Nile’s three seasons, look closely at two pieces of the harvest wall, finish a claim from sentence starters, and ask one question the sources leave open.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Complete an evidence chart for the four sources, explain what the harvest wall can and cannot show, and write a claim, evidence and reasoning paragraph.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Work out a rough date for the Great Pyramid from poster 1, compare it with the harvest wall, rate each source’s reach, and write an argument that answers the slave myth and names a limit of the evidence.

steps.purpose: Sort and weigh the sources, then make a claim from them, at the right level of challenge.
students: All three work from the same four sources and end with a claim.

steps.title: Teamwork
script: Students reread their notes from the hook. Ask two or three to say whether they would change their answer, and which source changed it. Red Level students give one limit of the evidence. Close with poster 1’s question: *“What is the biggest thing you have ever made or done with other people, and what made the teamwork easy or hard?”*

screen.question: Building a pyramid took thousands of people working together. What is the biggest thing you have ever made or done with other people?

steps.purpose: Return to the hook with evidence, then connect the builders’ teamwork to students’ own.
students: Look at your note from the start. Would you change it? Why?
What made the teamwork easy or hard?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
steps.purpose: Check what each student can now do against the objectives.
students: describe how the Nile shaped Egypt’s land and year?
explain who built the pyramids, with evidence?
say what each kind of source can and cannot show?
judge how far a later source can support a claim?
